title: Demonstrate an understanding of different wine cultivars

lessons.title: What a cultivar is and the main white cultivars
lessons.html:
What a cultivar is and the main white cultivars

A cultivar is a kind (variety) of grape plant. Each cultivar has its own leaves, bunches, berry colour, taste and ripening time. The wine made from it also has its own taste. A farm may grow many cultivars, and each block in the vineyard usually has one cultivar. Workers must know which cultivar is in which block, because pruning, spraying and harvest timing can be different.

White and red cultivars

White wine cultivars have green or yellow berries. Red wine cultivars have dark blue or black berries. Red wine gets its colour from the skins.

Important white cultivars in South Africa

CultivarThings to know
Chenin BlancThe most planted cultivar in South Africa, often called Steen. Grows well in many areas.
Sauvignon BlancLikes cooler sites. Fresh, green, grassy flavours.
ChardonnayUsed for still wine and sparkling wine (Méthode Cap Classique).
ColombarWidely grown in warmer inland areas such as Robertson and the Orange River; used for wine and brandy.
Muscat (Hanepoot)Sweet, perfumed grapes; used for sweet wines and also eaten as table grapes.

How to tell cultivars apart

You learn to recognise cultivars by looking at:

  • Leaves: shape, how deep the cuts (lobes) are, and whether they are hairy underneath.
  • Bunches: size and shape, loose or tight.
  • Berries: colour, size, round or oval, and taste.
  • Ripening time: some cultivars ripen early in summer, others late.

Block labels and the farm's vineyard map also show the cultivar. If you are unsure, ask your supervisor.

lessons.title: Red cultivars and why cultivar matters in the vineyard
lessons.html:
Red cultivars and why cultivar matters in the vineyard

Important red cultivars in South Africa

CultivarThings to know
Cabernet SauvignonSmall, dark berries with thick skins; ripens late; makes strong red wines.
Shiraz (Syrah)Grows well in warm areas; spicy wines.
PinotageA South African cultivar, bred at Stellenbosch University from Pinot Noir and Cinsaut (also called Hermitage).
MerlotSoft red wines; often blended with Cabernet Sauvignon.
CinsautLarge bunches; light, fruity wines.
Pinot NoirNeeds a cool site; thin skins; used for red wine and sparkling wine.

Why the cultivar matters for your work

  • Pruning: some cultivars bear fruit well on short spurs, others need longer canes. Your supervisor will tell you the method for each block.
  • Disease: cultivars with tight bunches and thin skins rot more easily. They need careful leaf removal and spraying.
  • Harvest time: early cultivars are picked first. Picking the wrong block at the wrong time spoils the wine.
  • Keeping cultivars apart: grapes from different cultivars must not be mixed in the same bin unless the cellar says so. Mixed loads can ruin a batch of wine.

Rootstocks

Most vines in South Africa are grafted. The top part (scion) is the wine cultivar. The bottom part (rootstock) is a different kind of vine that resists phylloxera, a tiny insect that kills vine roots. The rootstock also helps the vine cope with the soil. Any shoots growing from the rootstock below the graft must be removed (suckering).

Key points

  • A cultivar is a kind of grape plant with its own leaves, bunches, berries and wine taste.
  • Chenin Blanc is South Africa's most planted cultivar; Pinotage was bred in South Africa.
  • Recognise cultivars by leaves, bunches, berries and ripening time.
  • Pruning, spraying and harvest timing depend on the cultivar.
  • Never mix cultivars in one bin unless the cellar says so.
